newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end up on firm dlr, foreign buying.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end up on firm dlr, foreign buying.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed higher in technically-driven trade on Friday after a rising dollar encouraged domestic and foreign investors to purchase American debt securities, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 20/32 at 99-00. Its yield slipped to 6.58 percent against 6.62 percent in the previous session.
Market participants said the greenback strength triggered a buying spree sponsored by some local hedge funds and some Japanese trust funds.
In late Friday trade, the dollar was quoted at 1.5545 mark, above the highest weekly close in 1996 of 1.5475. The U.S. currency was also firm against the yen at 113.90 yen.
Portfolio managers, who are struggling to keep gains for 1996 after a recent strong drop in Treasury prices, were also perceived to be buyers in the long-end of the yield curve.

"A lot of people on Wall Street still have their bonuses on the line ... and many money managers just saw their (1996) gains being dramatically reduced with the recent selloff," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
"Those guys want to see this market go up," he added.
And that was exactely what the market did after falling for three consecutive sessions and ending another one little changed this week.

Analysts said the short end of the yield curve was helped by some buying from Asian investors looking for a safe-haven to park their money for the weekend after a sharp drop in stock prices in Tokyo and Hong Kong on Friday.
"Trading has been really technical and based on flows. Everyone is trying to square books at the end of the year," said the head of the Treasury trading desk at a U.S. commercial bank.
Players paid little attention to some fresh economic indicators released Friday, some of which actually carried positive news to the bond market.
Traders were pleased by a drop in the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index to 98.9 in the preliminary December reading against 99.2 in the final November.
Business inventories for October, also issued on Friday, jumped 0.5 percent, the biggest rise since the 0.6 percent increase in January 1996. Business sales were up 0.2 percent.
"The fundamental background hasn't changed much over the last week week or so," said Dana Johnson, managing director of research at First National Bank of Chicago.
"I think we're looking at data which suggest that inflation pressures are minimum, consumer spending is moderate at best and the labor markets are tight," he added.
Analysts said Treasuries are expected to trade within ranges over the next week as liquidity decreases ahead of the year-end holidays.
"I think we're going remain pretty much rangebound," said Josh Feinman, global markets economist at BT Securities.
Volume as measured by GovPX was at $82.4 billion in late trade, around 60 percent above average for an autumn Friday.
GovPX publishes real time Treasury prices and volume from five of the six intra-dealer brokers, representing 65 percent of the intra-dealers trades.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down two basis points at 4.80 percent. The six-month bill rate rose one point to 4.99 percent. The year bill rate was down three points at 5.15 percent.

The two-year note closed up 2/32 at 99-24/32, yielding 5.76 percent. The five-year note traded up 8/32 at 99-7/32 to yield 6.06 percent. The ten-year note closed up 14/32 at 101-10/32, yielding 6.32 percent.
